Frustration was all Jhoka had known since her mentor left her as she tried to apply the concepts Inzili taught her to the small tablet device that ran a program designed to teach young minds. Inzili had taught her how a "clock" worked, or at least how to read the dials, but Jhoka did not know how the human system of "numbers" worked and mathematics was something taught only to scholars on her world. Suddenly she had felt not only like a clumsy, awkward outcast but also extremely stupid and ignorant about things taught to mere children of other races. Stan's kind had mastered travel through the stars and powerful weapons that could end a life with a flash of thunder, her's had figured out how to throw spears. Her claws fumbled to input what the device asked of her as she glanced over at the markings made on a piece of paper, another invention she had never seen before, for reference on how the humans made numbers.

"Correct! Good work!" chirped the speakers on the small, handheld contraption, the screen flashed a splash of green objects to indicate a correct solution.

"Finally! Stupid thing," Jhoka muttered as she angrily ignored the tinny, alien voice speaking nonsense at her.

Even so, a success after so many failures brought a surge of relief. What was most confusing was how the process of time was divided, seconds, hours, and minutes were all strange, abstract things she had difficulty grasping when she couldn't see them. Jhoka could personally count up to however many claws she had, but she was vaguely aware of numbers and amounts beyond that but had no way to express it in her language. Looking at a clock meant dealing with those large amounts on a regular basis. Fortunately clocks were round and could be divided into parts, visible chunks that she herself could understand and the problems were oriented toward these sort of rough divisions.

After another tough hour she sat down the tablet and sighed, all ten simple problems were complete but she wasn't sure if she had learned anything.

"Reward time, I guess," she said softly as she gathered up her waiting sling and the collection of pebbles that she would use to secure more food.

Before she took off she remembered to grab that magic box with the stick coming out of it, the one that carried her voice far away. What she really wanted was the thunder stick the human had, but apparently it was too dangerous to handle and no amount of pleading would change the minds that had been made up. That didn't matter, she was good with a sling.

Jade and Inzili were up in the forward part of the ship working on the mechanical components that Jhoka didn't even begin to understand, Stan was outside doing the same but on the large bulges that protruded from the topside of the ship. Most of the ship had been torn apart, a process that was explained to Jhoka that she understood needed to happen after so many moons or else terrible things would happen. They were apparently in the process of putting it all back together, she was skeptical of the progress they claimed to have made, but either way the children were spending time with their mothers. That left her free to do whatever she wanted! Or she felt like it, at least.

Walking down the large ramp she inhaled a deep breath, smelling the breeze as she pulled it in. Being outside she could hear Stan on top the ship, the clanking of metal on metal likely being heard far away but likely not as far as the river. Thinking about the sounds Jhoka realized that the trees likely shielded a lot of what the breeze didn't carry off, and her nose told her that the prey was upwind anyway. Having a direction to go she bounded across the open grass as fast as her feet would take her, hoping to get in as much as she could while it was still daylight.

After a half hour of running she paused to catch her breath, the young hunter having traveled a remarkable distance in a short amount of time. Following her nose as she ran put her very close to a herd of small four-legged creatures that were locally known as "mauwaks." Being about the size of a dog had it's advantages on Jhoka's world, most of the large predators simply couldn't chase them through the brush and anything that would strike from the air was too large to fly through the trees. Using their long, lizard-like tail the mauwak could keep it's balance as it darted between the large tree trunks and it's wide shoulders and wide paws gave it further stability to make sudden changes in direction.

Unfortunately for the mauwak the indigenous people had developed projectile weapons.

Most of the native tribes used slings or boomerang-like hunting sticks to strike at the creatures, both of which negated their natural abilities of evasion. What was left for the mauwak was it's tough, leathery hide and a dense hedge of feathers that ran down it's spine from it's head to the tail to shrug off blows. Additionally the jaws and skull had a mane of sorts of small feathers that were used for non-verbal communication, on males it concealed patches of red used to attract mates. These posed problems for light or low-velocity projectiles, which is why the peoples who relied mostly on mauwaks for hides and meats used special hunting spears meant for throwing.

One of the northernmost villages of the Nine Lodge Clan were made up of the people who came from the frosty lands long ago, they were ethnically different than Jhoka's tribe and only bound by marriage and a complex web of kinship ties. Through them she saw this weapon at work during the hunting games, thrown with such force and precision that it blinded a mighty raunaua and let the others make the kill with the long spears.

Virgins were of low class in her society and she had not been allowed to participate in that noble hunt, but she was allowed to keep watch with the males who did the work of butchering it after the gigantic beast was dead. Then the hunters fanned out to stop the scavengers, a raunaua corpse was a lot of meat in the summer sun and it attracted all kinds of things with sharp teeth. Others with less status or in their twilight years stood by to help, using whatever they could to keep the circling wildlife. That was where she was best anyway, she didn't know anyone who could swing a sling better than she could which gave her a cutting edge in keeping hungry scavengers away. She learned to do that hunting the mawuak, it was how she maintained her place in the village.

First she found a good position to fire from, crouching low to remain out of sight, and she loaded her sling with the first rock while a second was clutched in her throwing hand and a third in her offhand. Jhoka's secret was to wait after setting up, unlike most animals on her planet the mauwak often deliberately hid it's distress and communicated potential threats by a "war-wah" noise it interjected between the "mau-wak" croaks it was named for. After a few seconds of tensing her body to get the muscles ready Jhoka popped up as she started her swinging, releasing before she was fully upright.

Usually her first shot was the weakest but it was quite deadly this time, the second-closest mauwak, a large male, suddenly lurched forward with a gentle grunt; dead from a sharp blow to the head.

Dropping the rock into her sling took no time or effort, she had practiced this ever since she was a small girl and could do it with her eyes closed; indeed she didn't even look at her sling as she did it then. Panic had not yet spread throughout the herd but the closest female had seen the male fall and paused to think, suddenly it dawned on her that the male was indeed dead and she screeched a loud cry to indicate alarm to the rest of the herd but it was cut short as she turned. Jhoka smirked as her second stone found it's mark and loaded a third into the sling, but by this time the herd was scrambling around to figure out a direction to run and picking a target was almost impossible. After a few tense seconds she saw an opportunity and started up the swing, standing for better control as she swung harder and harder before releasing the stone that, after a second of travel, cracked a third mauwak square in the base of the skull at the last possible second.

"You won't get away!" she exclaimed, leaping over the bush and sprinting over to the flailing creature as he tried to regain his sense of balance.

Unfortunately for the creature her skilled hands drove the steel alloy knife Stan had given her deep into it's brain from a soft spot behind the jaws, killing the hapless creature in a single blow.

"Sorry, I wished you had died without pain," she said softly as she let the final beats of it's heart pulse blood out of the neck wound.

Letting the excitement in her body took a few minutes, but in that time she silently thanked the Goddess for a successful hunt and thought about what she wanted to take back. The first male and the female were both quite large and very plump, their wide hips were wrapped in succulent cuts of marbled flesh and cream-colored fat. That second male she had taken was also quite large, but leaner and when she groped underneath the thigh it was clear he wasn't long into adulthood and hadn't built up a lot of muscle. Too bad!

Still, Jhoka was faced with a dilemma.

Since she had run so very far she had to inevitably carry back what she had killed, normally this wouldn't be an issue with a pack of hunters who would split the load up among themselves. Unfortunately she was alone and mauwaks were heavy creatures and, in her excitement, she killed two of the largest ones in the herd! After realizing just how heavy they were she sighed, wiggling her fingers into the creature's mouth as she dragged it by the snout over to the other two. Then she rolled them on their backs and stretched them out to get a good look at them, but unfortunately it just made her feel even smaller seeing so much flesh.

So we homeschool our oldest is 4 and we do classical education anyone else homeschool? 8f so what are some helpful tips?

Not homeschooling as I don't have kids yet, but I was homeschooled and I will homeschool my kids.

Biggest thing is structure in field trips and actually do stuff. My Dad and I always went to museums and mom and I would do art classes together. I have great memories and we still do that stuff.

Vary the curriculum and expose your kids to new ideas. Encourage them to think for themselves. I had all types of stuff, Mom would occasionally let me choose filler subjects. I learned calligraphy and botany and fun stuff like that. I suck at math and had to repeat the same stuff over and over, so expect that.

Mom tested us with the Iowa and California standardized tests back when they didn't suck. Consider seeking out similar tests to see where your little ones are. We were in trouble if we were anything besides "exceeding".

We schooled all year round and ended up being 3 years ahead. My sister and I both enrolled in college early and graduated with our BA's 3 years in advance. I've been working my way up in healthcare for 5 years and she is going to be awarded her PhD in December. It's easier to school when you aren't retracing things because the kids were on break and forgot it. Being ahead gave us such a head start and made us candidates for academic scholarships. Neither of us have debt thanks to Mama pushing us so hard.

Be strict. Don't let your kids slack off. Join a group if you have one in your area. Let your little one pick a hobby like art, a sport, anything they can have that is theirs. That will help them make friends and hold their own. Sometimes it's not easy being the homeschool kid, but they will be better for it.

Just love them. I fought my mom when I was younger but my life would be completely different if she didn't sacrifice and push us like she did.

We do. At that age there are not many tips I can give you except make certain learning is active, fun, and hands on as much as possible. Is there something in particular you are concerned about?

I just don't want my kids to ever feel behind the rest of the re age group so I'm always worried that if I fall behind or if I don't teach the right way that they will fall behind and not get something that is important. I try to make things fun by making every experience we have a learning one.

You get what you pay for in terms of curriculum. Easy pezzy is free, but the amount of time you spend augmenting it with more rigorous material is almost not worth the free price. We love Singapore Math and use Trivium for logic, reasoning, grammar. When your kid's old enough consider Science Olympiad as a way to augment science curriculum. Some parents in our area use science Olympiad as their only science courses throughout the year- they get very deep understanding on topics that way, compete against the smartest kids in your state, and it looks great on a college application.

Also, if you're not religious, most curriculum has a lot of religious components built in, so you'll need to decide how much to keep in as comparative literature or strip out and add your own material.

You're biggest challenge will be keeping your children from being socially awkward. I was homeschooled my wife was homeschooled and we didn't have a problem, but the other homeschool kids I have met do seem to have trouble socially because they were pretty well sheltered.

Look for a homeschool group in your area. There is bound to be at least one close to you. This will help with field trips and social activities. At the very least the other parents there will probably have children around your child's age so you can set up play dates.

If your kid wants to get involved with band or sports you should be able to find a music school that has a small band and you can sign your kid up for little leagues without school affiliation. When they get older and want to play highschool sports call the school your children would have gone to and they may work something out so your children can play.

There are so many options for curriculum out there now that you need to heavily research before buying one. Don't slack on reading lists and since you're picking what they read you can skip some of the books you didn't enjoy on the list and replace them with another.

When they are about middle school age start looking at options for college, if they want to go. There are many universities that have great scholarships for homeschoolers that could be overlooked if your not careful.

Maintain structure and don't forget about physical education. Make sure they get exercise and play outside.

Don't completely lock them down shutting out the entire world because when they get 18 they will let all that angst out in one huge wild ride and may not stop.

Hi! I homeschool my 8-yr-old son and 10-yr-old daughter and always have. We have used workbooks in the past, but we have pretty much always done classical education. We use Singapore Math (standards) --highly recommend Singapore. We use lots of materials from Classical Academic Press: Reading and Reasoning, Writing and Rhetoric, Latin for Children, and Well Ordered Language. We use the Story of the World series with the corresponding activity books. The workbooks that we've used in the past were from Seton Press, but we just don't have time for filling out worksheets any more. We do use some of Seton's art history books and history books. I use the Spalding Method too, even though it's super daunting and a lot of work--it's worth it. My kids do copywork. They learn cursive writing. We buy science kits. I read-aloud advanced Classic books to my kids and have them read the Classics themselves too in their entirety (not just excerpts). We've done classical homeschooling co-ops before. We go year-round with breaks for religious holidays/holy days and summer camps.

Helpful tips that I've learned: re-evaluate the materials and activity schedule every year. Get music lessons for your kid. Join co-ops. Take advantage of summer camps to socialize the kid but also give you your own "vacation" from teaching too. Sign them up for sports (husband and I are not sports people, but the exercise and social skills that our kids get are worth it). Take advantage of "vacation Bible school"; they're usually free, and you know your kid is going to learn some good morals. Also don't forget to have fun too! It's easy to get burned out on homeschooling if there isn't a balance of fun for us Moms too.

At this point, my daughter wakes herself up at 6 a.m., eats breakfast while doing her writing, and then tackles everything else that she possibly can while I'm still in the shower or drinking my coffee. She likes to get her work done in a few hours and then have the rest of the day to read, play violin, paint, or work on her calligraphy. My son is usually still laying on the floor when I'm done with my coffee, and sometimes it takes him hours to finish his Math work--but homeschooling works out nicely for him too, because if he wants to waste playtime by dragging out his work, then we have all the time in the world. It's only his own time that he's wasting (to a point, obviously; privileges are taken away if it gets out of hand). He's getting better about doing his work diligently as he gets older though.

I like to re-evaluate our decision to homeschool every year. We're moving soon to an area with nice private schools, and even one with a classical school. However, when I saw that their curriculum was so very similar to our own but with a $10k/yr price tag, I just can't help but re-affirm our homeschooling decision as a prudent, fiscally-responsible choice.

GLHF

You're welcome! At this point, with a 4-yr-old, you could get the Spalding Method: Writing Road to Reading book and start going through it yourself (my book is all marked up and flagged). You could get some Orton cards (is that what they're called?) or Spalding phonogram cards and start going through the various sounds per alphabet letter. Read-alouds that my kids enjoyed at that age were the Narnia books and Watership Down. I think I bought some preschool general math books from the bookstore at that age just to familiarize them with numbers and counting and writing numbers (nothing extensive). We did a lot of playgroups at that age--which isn't too early to start joining homeschool groups either, considering many states are funding 4K programs now (so other 4-yr-olds are in a school setting already and not on the playground to play with your kid in the morning). You'll figure it all out soon enough--that's half the fun!

I wish you the best in your homeschooling adventure!
